narrativeBlocks.title: The scene
narrativeBlocks.body: After the killing of his children in madness, Heracles receives an oracle directing service to Eurystheus. The initial instruction is ten labours; the familiar total becomes twelve when Eurystheus refuses to count two feats.

narrativeBlocks.title: What the source does
narrativeBlocks.body: Source quotation (translation; whitespace normalized): “Now it came to pass that after the battle with the Minyans Hercules was driven mad through the jealousy of Hera and flung his own children, whom he had by Megara, and two children of Iphicles into the fire; wherefore he condemned himself to exile, and was purified by Thespius, and repairing to Delphi”

narrativeBlocks.title: Why it matters
narrativeBlocks.body: Interpretation: The catalogue creates a readable system, but that order is a later mythographic construction rather than a single original script.

narrativeBlocks.title: Read it carefully
narrativeBlocks.body: Do not start with the familiar total and assume the source begins there. Distinguish the oracle’s ten tasks from the eventual twelve, and ask how Eurystheus’ judgement shapes the catalogue.

narrativeBlocks.title: Carry it forward
narrativeBlocks.body: Read the next labours as problems of method, not only feats of strength.

quiz.prompt: Why does the catalogue eventually reach twelve?

choices.text: Eurystheus refuses the Hydra labour because Iolaus helped and the Augeas labour because it was for hire.
Heracles performs two extra labours after being received among the gods.
The Pythian priestess revises her oracle after Heracles reaches Tiryns.

quiz.explanation: The Library gives two distinct reasons: Iolaus helped with the Hydra, and the Augeas task was performed for hire.
